before.childHint: Look at the words in the question. Are things getting bigger, smaller, or being shared?
before.description: Adding instead of subtracting, multiplying instead of dividing, or vice versa.

after.description: Adding instead of subtracting, multiplying instead of dividing, or vice versa.
after.childHint: Before you work it out, decide what each step needs: add, take away, multiply or divide. Then check that your answer has grown or shrunk the way it should.

before.childHint: Percent means "out of 100". It is a proportion, not an exact amount of money!
before.description: Subtracting the percentage digits directly as pounds or pence.

after.description: Subtracting the percentage digits directly as pounds or pence.
after.childHint: Percent means "out of 100". The percent is a share of the amount, not a number to take away from it!

before.childHint: The decimal point separates wholes from parts. Compare the parts column by column, starting with the tenths.
before.description: Thinking 3.12 is larger than 3.8 because 12 is bigger than 8.

after.description: Thinking 3.12 is larger than 3.8 because 12 is bigger than 8.
after.childHint: The decimal point separates wholes from parts. Read each digit after the point in its own column, not as one whole number.

before.childHint: Check the columns carefully. Ones, tens, hundreds, thousands. Which column does that digit actually sit in?
before.description: Child gives 60 for the 6 in 4,652 where the answer is 600, reading the digit one column to the right; or 6,000, reading it one column to the left.

after.description: Child gives 60 for the 6 in 4,652 where the answer is 600, reading the digit one column to the right; or 6,000, reading it one column to the left.
after.childHint: Check the columns carefully. Name every column, counting out from the ones. Which column does that digit actually sit in?

before.childHint: Ask what the angles sit on first. A line is 180, a turn is 360.
before.description: Uses the wrong total for the shape, typically 360 for a straight line or a triangle, or 90 for a straight line.

after.description: Uses the wrong total for the shape, typically 360 for a straight line or a triangle, or 90 for a straight line.
after.childHint: First ask what the angles make: a straight line, a triangle or a full turn. A line and a triangle both make 180°, and a full turn makes 360°.

before.childHint: Check how strong the word is. A quiet word needs a quiet answer.
before.description: Picks a word from the right family at the wrong intensity, far stronger or far weaker than the headword (terrified for TIMID; annoyed for FURIOUS).

after.description: Picks a word from the right family at the wrong intensity, far stronger or far weaker than the headword (terrified for TIMID; annoyed for FURIOUS).
after.childHint: Some words say a lot and some say a little. Choose the answer that says just as much as the word you are given.

before.childHint: A true opposite flips the meaning exactly, like hot and cold.
before.description: Chose a loosely different word, not a true opposite.

after.description: Chose a loosely different word, not a true opposite.
after.childHint: A true opposite flips the meaning exactly, like open and shut.

before.childHint: Pop the letter into the second word and say it aloud. Does it sound like a real word?
before.description: Chose a letter that does not make a real second word when added.

after.description: Chose a letter that does not make a real second word when added.
after.childHint: Pop the letter into the second word, trying every spot. Does any spot make a real word?

before.childHint: Draw the arrow: which way did the first pair travel?
before.description: Moved backwards through the alphabet instead of forwards.

after.description: Moved the opposite way through the alphabet to the first pair.
after.childHint: Check which way the first pair moves along the alphabet. Go the same way from the new letter.

before.childHint: This gap wants a or an. Say the next word aloud. Which sound starts it?
before.description: On an a or an choice, picks the to avoid the vowel-sound judgement. The fits any noun without a sound decision, so the child reaches for the article that asks nothing of her ear.

after.description: On an a or an choice, picks the to avoid the vowel-sound judgement. The fits any noun without a sound decision, so the child reaches for the article that asks nothing of her ear.
after.childHint: This gap wants a or an. Hear the next word in your head. Which sound starts it?

before.childHint: Look at where the example word takes its letters from. Copy those exact positions.
before.description: Took letters from the middle instead of the shown positions.

after.description: Took letters from other places in the outer words instead of the positions the example shows.
after.childHint: Look at where the example word takes its letters from. Copy those exact positions.
